claims.text: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The greater local lattice distortion in the quinary alloy modifies its stacking-fault energy.
Changes in stacking-fault energy alter dislocation mobility and deformation-twinning behavior.
The quinary alloy has enhanced work hardening and delayed failure relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The alloys can be compared in equiatomic, single-phase FCC states produced by identical thermomechanical processing.
The controlled comparison will use identical processing followed by room-temperature, quasi-static tensile testing.
X-ray diffraction and microscopy will be used to confirm a comparable single-phase FCC microstructure.
Local lattice distortion and associated stacking-fault-energy changes affect dislocation-core spreading.
Local lattice distortion and associated stacking-fault-energy changes affect activation of deformation twinning.
The additional constituent in the quinary alloy produces greater lattice-strain heterogeneity.
Greater lattice-strain heterogeneity raises barriers to dislocation slip.
The quinary alloy's lattice distortion and stacking-fault-energy state promote deformation twinning.
Greater slip resistance and increased twinning produce higher work hardening and greater ductility before failure.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower work-hardening rates.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have less pronounced lattice distortion and higher effective stacking-fault energies than the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy will show superior strength and delayed onset of failure mechanisms.
The hypothesis is restricted to comparable single-phase FCC alloys tested in room-temperature, quasi-static tension.
Quantitative differences in strength, work hardening, and twinning may depend on compositional fluctuations and processing history.

Failure to observe statistically significant increases in the proposed mechanical responses, associated changes in dislocation or twinning behavior, or reduced stacking-fault energy in the quinary alloy would falsify the proposed explanation.
